Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "last thursday i went to the alder creek reserve field station for a meeting about the camera traps, and it was supposed to begin at nine but the gravel road was wet and i got there at 9:12. the station is a converted equipment shed beside the old cattle gate, with a tin roof that makes conversation hard when rain is coming down. mara ellis, the reserve technician, was there with a map spread over a folding table, and jonah price from the county wildlife office had brought a laptop and a plastic case of spare parts. lee, a volunteer who checks the north trail units, came in carrying a thermos and a damp notebook. there were four of us, though mara said the district biologist might join by phone later. no call came during the meeting.

we had eight cameras out along the creek and the oak ridge, but only six were producing files that could be opened. one unit at the lower ford had taken pictures with a pale stripe across the bottom, which jonah thought could be a loose seal or water on the lens. he did not know which, and the housing looked dry when lee checked it the day before. another camera near the ridge had a blank card, even though its battery indicator showed two bars. mara said it could have been a card problem, but she had not tested it yet. the two cameras that were offline were both on the east side, where the trail crosses a patch of loose shale. we talked about whether the slope had shifted their mounts, but no one had visited those two locations since the previous rain.

mara pointed to a cluster of red dots on the map and explained that those were the places where deer had been recorded most often since january. the dates on the printed sheet were not all comparable, because one camera had been moved in february and another had been running only on alternate nights to save battery. lee said, “i keep seeing the same buck by the north trail, but i can't tell if it's the same one every time.” he had noticed a short fork in the right antler in three images, although the dates were nine days apart and the angles were different. jonah asked that we avoid calling it an individual animal in the spreadsheet until someone could check more frames. the group agreed to enter those records as “adult deer, identity uncertain.”

1. before the next round of checks, we listed the things that needed attention. the lower ford camera needed its lens and seal looked at, and the ridge camera needed a card test before we decided the unit itself was faulty. the two east-side units needed a visit to see whether the mounts were still stable. mara wanted the batteries measured with the handheld tester, not just read from the small display, because the display had been inconsistent on cold mornings. lee noted that the north trail camera was angled a little low after he had cleared a branch from its view. he could not remember whether he had tightened the strap again afterward, so he offered to check it while he was there. we did not assign a date for the whole round because the forecast was changing, and jonah said he would email the access schedule once he heard back about a road repair crew.

we also spent time on how the cameras were configured. the units were set for three photographs in a burst, with a ten-second quiet period before another trigger, except the creek unit, which was set to video for short clips. mara said she had chosen that setting because water movement was setting off too many pictures at night. the clip files were much larger, and the memory card filled sooner than she expected. jonah suggested lowering the video length from twenty seconds to fifteen, but he said he wanted to compare the settings sheet first. nobody changed a setting during the meeting. lee asked if the infrared flash was visible to animals, and mara said it was described as low-glow, but she did not know whether deer could see it. she said the manual might answer that, and the manual was in a drawer at the station.

when we looked at the fox pictures, there were twelve usable frames from the creek camera over three nights. in four of them the fox was carrying something small, but the object was too blurred to identify. lee thought it might be a rodent; mara said it could also be a piece of bark because the tail end was not visible. we left the entry as “small item, unclear.” a separate image showed a raccoon passing behind the same log at 2:41 a.m. the date stamp was correct on that camera, while the ridge unit had been about seven minutes slow on the last check. jonah said clock drift could matter when we compared images between locations, especially if an animal crossed both paths in one night. he asked us to record the displayed time before resetting any clock, rather than correcting it from memory.

before leaving, mara opened the supply cupboard and counted four new straps, two weather covers, and one unopened pack of lithium batteries. there were also three partly used battery sets in a labeled tub, but the labels only gave the month they had been removed, not which cameras they came from. lee said he could add camera numbers to the labels on his next visit, if he had a marker that would write on the plastic. jonah put the spare memory cards back in their sleeves and wrote “tested” on one sleeve, although he had not yet tested that card; he corrected the note to “for testing” after mara pointed it out. the table map stayed behind at the station, marked with the six working units in green pencil and the two unverified east-side locations in orange.", "output": "Last Thursday, I went to the Alder Creek Reserve field station for a meeting about the camera traps. It was supposed to begin at nine, but the gravel road was wet, and I arrived at 9:12. The station is a converted equipment shed beside the old cattle gate, with a tin roof that makes conversation difficult when rain is coming down. Mara Ellis, the reserve technician, was there with a map spread over a folding table, and Jonah Price from the county wildlife office had brought a laptop and a plastic case of spare parts. Lee, a volunteer who checks the north trail units, came in carrying a thermos and a damp notebook. There were four of us, although Mara said the district biologist might join by phone later. No call came during the meeting.

We had eight cameras out along the creek and the oak ridge, but only six were producing files that could be opened. One unit at the lower ford had taken pictures with a pale stripe across the bottom. Jonah thought it might be a loose seal or water on the lens, but he did not know which. The housing looked dry when Lee checked it the day before. Another camera near the ridge had a blank card, even though its battery indicator showed two bars. Mara said it could be a card problem, but she had not tested it yet. The two cameras that were offline were both on the east side, where the trail crosses a patch of loose shale. We discussed whether the slope had shifted their mounts, but no one had visited those locations since the previous rain.

Mara pointed to a cluster of red dots on the map and explained that those were the places where deer had been recorded most often since January. The dates on the printed sheet were not all comparable because one camera had been moved in February and another had been running only on alternate nights to save battery. Lee said, “I keep seeing the same buck by the north trail, but I can't tell if it's the same one every time.” He had noticed a short fork in the right antler in three images, although the dates were nine days apart and the angles were different. Jonah asked us not to call it an individual animal in the spreadsheet until someone could check more frames. The group agreed to enter those records as “adult deer, identity uncertain.”

1. Before the next round of checks, we listed the items that needed attention. The lower ford camera needed its lens and seal checked, and the ridge camera needed a card test before we decided the unit itself was faulty. The two east-side units needed a visit to see whether their mounts were still stable. Mara wanted the batteries measured with the handheld tester, not just read from the small display, because the display had been inconsistent on cold mornings. Lee noted that the north trail camera was angled a little low after he had cleared a branch from its view. He could not remember whether he had tightened the strap again afterward, so he offered to check it while he was there. We did not assign a date for the whole round because the forecast was changing, and Jonah said he would email the access schedule once he heard back about a road repair crew.

We also spent time discussing how the cameras were configured. The units were set for three photographs in a burst, with a ten-second quiet period before another trigger, except for the creek unit, which was set to record short video clips. Mara said she had chosen that setting because water movement was triggering too many pictures at night. The clip files were much larger, and the memory card filled sooner than she expected. Jonah suggested lowering the video length from twenty seconds to fifteen, but said he wanted to compare the settings sheet first. Nobody changed a setting during the meeting. Lee asked whether the infrared flash was visible to animals, and Mara said it was described as low-glow, but she did not know whether deer could see it. She said the manual might answer that; it was in a drawer at the station.

When we looked at the fox pictures, there were twelve usable frames from the creek camera over three nights. In four of them, the fox was carrying something small, but the object was too blurred to identify. Lee thought it might be a rodent; Mara said it could also be a piece of bark because the tail end was not visible. We left the entry as “small item, unclear.” A separate image showed a raccoon passing behind the same log at 2:41 a.m. The date stamp was correct on that camera, while the ridge unit had been about seven minutes slow at the last check. Jonah said clock drift could matter when we compared images between locations, especially if an animal crossed both paths in one night. He asked us to record the displayed time before resetting any clock rather than correcting it from memory.

Before leaving, Mara opened the supply cupboard and counted four new straps, two weather covers, and one unopened pack of lithium batteries. There were also three partly used battery sets in a labeled tub, but the labels gave only the month they had been removed, not the cameras they came from. Lee said he could add camera numbers to the labels on his next visit if he had a marker that would write on the plastic. Jonah put the spare memory cards back in their sleeves and wrote “tested” on one sleeve, although he had not tested that card yet. He corrected the note to “for testing” after Mara pointed it out. The table map stayed behind at the station, marked with the six working units in green pencil and the two unverified east-side locations in orange."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-polish-0280", "row_sha256": "885636e13eb4b76f409e66e60381a7584882cfc5780b042fde4aecb7d0d3213b", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. we set the camera traps along the alder creek loop after the first frost, when the ground was firm enough to reach the north bank without leaving deep ruts. the loop is about 1.8 kilometers, and it passes through mixed spruce, alder and a small patch of wet meadow. we wanted to compare animal visits at the creek crossing with visits along the drier ridge, not to estimate how many animals live in the whole valley. that distinction mattered when we picked stations: each camera records one narrow view, and a busy frame is not automatically a busy population.

before carrying anything out, we looked at the old field map and checked it against the creek after the summer flood. one trail marked on the map now ended at a pile of willow branches, so we did not use that spot. we chose six stations, three near the water and three on the ridge, with roughly 300 meters between cameras. the distances were not perfectly equal because the slope and thick brush made some places hard to approach quietly. at each site we noted the nearest trail, a recognizable tree, and the direction back to the loop. those notes helped us find the locations again without putting bright flagging around the cameras.

we carried the cameras, lock boxes, straps, spare batteries, memory cards, a small ruler, compass, notebook and a hand lens. before leaving the vehicle, we checked that every camera had the same date format and the clock was within two minutes of the field phone. the phone time was our reference, although we knew the camera clocks could drift during the deployment. we set each unit to take three photographs when its sensor was triggered, with a 20-second delay before it could trigger again. video was off because the memory cards were modest in size and our main comparison depended on photographs. we kept the same settings at all six stations so that later differences would not simply come from different camera choices.

at a station, we looked for a stable trunk about four to six meters from an animal path. we avoided trees that leaned over the water or shook noticeably in the wind. the camera went about 45 centimeters above the ground, aimed slightly downward, and pointed north or south where the site allowed it. aiming away from east and west reduced direct sun glare in the afternoon and morning, though it could not prevent every bright patch. we cleared only leaves and stems that covered the immediate view; we did not cut branches to make a better-looking opening. “leave the place looking ordinary,” Mara said, and that became our reminder not to turn a camera station into a clearing.

1. we strapped the camera to the trunk, tightened the lock box, and checked that the lens and sensor were not blocked by the box edge. then we measured the distance from the camera to a stick placed at the likely crossing point. the ruler in the frame gave us a reference for animal size and position; it was not intended to measure an animal in every photograph. we walked across the view at the expected path, then waited for the test images to appear. if a branch moved across the frame or the background was mostly blank sky, we adjusted the angle and tested again. once the view was usable, we removed the test images and wrote down that we had done so.

we recorded the station code, date, time, coordinates from the phone, camera height, direction, distance to the crossing point, card number and battery level. the phone coordinates were useful for returning, but we treated them as approximate under dense spruce. in the notebook we also described the ground: damp needles, exposed roots, mud, or a thin crust of snow. those details could matter when we later compared tracks with photographs, but we did not use tracks alone to declare an animal visit. at the creek stations, we noted water level against a marked rock. it was a simple reference, not a full stream gauge.

we left the units for 18 nights, except that station C4 stopped responding after the eleventh night. we found no obvious damage there, and its battery reading at the end was low. we could not tell from that reading whether cold weather, repeated triggers, or a weak battery had caused the stop. we replaced the batteries and card, checked the test images, and recorded the service time. the other cameras were not opened during the deployment. when two stations seemed to show the same animal moving along the creek, we wrote that as a possible sequence, not as proof that the pictures showed the same individual.

at retrieval, we noted the final time on each camera before removing its card. cards went into separate labeled sleeves, and we kept the station code with each file folder when copying the images. we made a second copy on the field laptop before clearing any card. a blank card did not mean there had been no animals: the camera might have missed them, the sensor might not have triggered, or an animal might have crossed outside the view. we also kept photographs that were blurry, partly blocked, or difficult to identify, marking them for review rather than silently deleting them. “uncertain is still a useful label,” Mara said while checking the creek files.

after the fieldwork, we planned to review photographs by station and time, note the visible species only when identification was clear enough, and flag uncertain images for a second look. we would report the number of independent camera events using the same separation rule at every station; a burst of three pictures from one trigger would remain one event. the records could describe activity at these six locations during this deployment. they could not, by themselves, establish total animal numbers, explain why an animal chose one route, or show that the pattern would hold in another season. if we repeat the work, we should keep the camera settings and station positions consistent where possible, and note any unavoidable change rather than treating the two deployments as perfectly identical.", "output": "MODE: /polish

we set the camera traps along the Alder Creek loop after the first frost, when the ground was firm enough to reach the north bank without leaving deep ruts. The loop is about 1.8 kilometers long and passes through mixed spruce and alder forest, as well as a small patch of wet meadow. We wanted to compare animal visits at the creek crossing with visits along the drier ridge, not estimate how many animals live in the whole valley. That distinction mattered when we chose the stations: each camera records a narrow view, and a busy frame does not automatically indicate a large population.

Before carrying anything into the field, we reviewed the old field map and checked it against the creek after the summer flood. One trail marked on the map now ended at a pile of willow branches, so we did not use that spot. We chose six stations, three near the water and three on the ridge, with roughly 300 meters between cameras. The distances were not perfectly equal because the slope and thick brush made some sites difficult to approach quietly. At each site, we noted the nearest trail, a recognizable tree, and the direction back to the loop. These notes helped us find the locations again without placing bright flagging around the cameras.

We carried the cameras, lock boxes, straps, spare batteries, memory cards, a small ruler, a compass, a notebook, and a hand lens. Before leaving the vehicle, we checked that every camera used the same date format and that its clock was within two minutes of the field phone. The phone time was our reference, although we knew the camera clocks might drift during deployment. We set each unit to take three photographs when triggered, with a 20-second delay before it could trigger again. We turned off video because the memory cards were modest in size and our main comparison depended on photographs. We kept the same settings at all six stations so that later differences would not simply reflect different camera choices.

At each station, we looked for a stable trunk about four to six meters from an animal path. We avoided trees that leaned over the water or shook noticeably in the wind. We mounted each camera about 45 centimeters above the ground, aimed it slightly downward, and pointed it north or south where the site allowed. Aiming away from east and west reduced direct sun glare in the afternoon and morning, though it could not prevent every bright patch. We cleared only the leaves and stems that obstructed the immediate view; we did not cut branches to create a better-looking opening. “Leave the place looking ordinary,” Mara said, and that became our reminder not to turn a camera station into a clearing.

1. We strapped the camera to the trunk, tightened the lock box, and checked that the box edge did not block the lens or sensor. Then we measured the distance from the camera to a stick placed at the likely crossing point. The ruler in the frame gave us a reference for animal size and position; it was not intended to measure an animal in every photograph. We walked across the view along the expected path, then waited for the test images to appear. If a branch moved across the frame or the background showed mostly blank sky, we adjusted the angle and tested again. Once the view was usable, we removed the test images and recorded that we had done so.

We recorded the station code, date, time, phone coordinates, camera height, direction, distance to the crossing point, card number, and battery level. The phone coordinates were useful for returning, but we treated them as approximate under dense spruce. In the notebook, we also described the ground: damp needles, exposed roots, mud, or a thin crust of snow. Those details could matter when we later compared tracks with photographs, but we did not use tracks alone to declare an animal visit. At the creek stations, we noted the water level against a marked rock. It was a simple reference, not a full stream gauge.

We left the units in place for 18 nights, except that station C4 stopped responding after the eleventh night. We found no obvious damage there, and its battery reading was low at the end. We could not tell from that reading whether cold weather, repeated triggers, or a weak battery had caused the stop. We replaced the batteries and card, checked the test images, and recorded the service time. We did not open the other cameras during deployment. When two stations seemed to show the same animal moving along the creek, we described it as a possible sequence, not proof that the pictures showed the same individual.

At retrieval, we noted each camera’s final time before removing its card. We placed the cards in separate labeled sleeves and kept the station code with each file folder when copying the images. We made a second copy on the field laptop before clearing any card. A blank card did not mean there had been no animals: a camera might have missed them, its sensor might not have triggered, or an animal might have crossed outside the view. We also kept photographs that were blurry, partly blocked, or difficult to identify, marking them for review rather than silently deleting them. “Uncertain is still a useful label,” Mara said while checking the creek files.

After the fieldwork, we planned to review photographs by station and time, record visible species only when identification was clear enough, and flag uncertain images for a second look. We would report the number of independent camera events using the same separation rule at every station; a burst of three pictures from one trigger would remain one event. The records could describe activity at these six locations during this deployment. On their own, they could not establish total animal numbers, explain why an animal chose one route, or show that the pattern would hold in another season.
